Revised assessment: The FOMC’s 25 bp cut to 1.50–1.75% and its directive to purchase Treasury bills and conduct repo operations to maintain ample reserves signal a deliberately dovish stance aimed at cushioning weakness in business fixed investment and exports while inflation runs below target. Standard business-cycle and investment literature emphasizes that declines in investment are a key driver of output fluctuations and can account for slowdowns in real GDP (investment function/accelerator mechanisms), so the Committee’s easing is consistent with stabilizing output in the face of firm-level capex softness. With market-based inflation compensation low and survey expectations little changed, the expectations channel matters: expected inflation influences current inflation and nominal rates (Cagan 1956; Rudebusch; Galí, Gertler, and López-Salido), so easing helps guard against expectations drifting down. The liquidity effect provides a near-term boost to aggregate demand when policy rates fall and reserves are added via open-market operations (monetary theory/Hume; Sims and Zha on monetary shocks’ real effects). At the same time, strong job gains and a low unemployment rate keep the near-term outlook supported (consistent with models where labor supply and employment drive output), though two dissents to holding rates underscore residual uncertainty about the appropriate degree of accommodation. On balance, the tone is cautiously positive: solid household spending and labor markets offset by weak investment/exports and sub-2% inflation, with policy easing appropriately leaning against downside risks (McCallum and Nelson 1999; Taylor 1983 critiques on stance).
